missions.title: Choose the right status

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: Start with a fresh function rather than a repair. A conditional selects behavior from the contract. Explain an exact-boundary example to yourself before writing code.

missions.title: Stay inside the window

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `and` requires both conditions to be true. Write each comparison as a full expression. Python also supports chained comparisons, such as `low <= value <= high`; both forms are valid.
lesson.code:
age = 18
paid = True
print(age >= 16 and paid)  # True

missions.brief: Return whether `value` falls inside the inclusive interval from `low` to `high`.
requirements: All inputs are integers and `low <= high`. Both endpoints belong to the interval. Return a Boolean.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: A value can fail at either end.
Passing just one boundary test is not sufficient.
Combine the lower-bound and upper-bound conditions, or use a chained comparison.

missions.title: Allow either route

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `or` requires at least one condition to be true. Its inclusive meaning includes the case where both are true. For this task the supplied flags are actual Boolean values.
lesson.code:
is_weekend = False
is_holiday = True
print(is_weekend or is_holiday)  # True

missions.brief: Return whether a visitor may enter using a ticket or staff access.
requirements: Both inputs are Booleans. Either a ticket or staff status allows entry, including when both are present. Return a Boolean.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
missions.example:

can_enter(False, True) -> True
hints: Which combinations should be denied?
Either successful access route is enough.
Check the both-true case as well as the two one-true cases.

missions.title: Block maintenance mode

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `not` reverses a truth value. Naming a flag clearly helps you decide whether the requirement needs it directly or negated. Parentheses can make combinations easier to read.

missions.brief: Return whether a connected device may start while respecting maintenance mode.
requirements: Inputs are Booleans. Starting requires connection and requires maintenance to be off. Return a Boolean.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.

can_start(True, True) -> False
hints: One flag describes permission; the other describes a blocker.

missions.title: Classify the reading

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: An `if/elif/else` chain runs the first matching branch. Broad conditions placed too early can swallow more specific cases. A small set of boundary examples helps establish the order.

missions.brief: Return the battery band for a supplied percentage.
requirements: `percent` is an integer from 0 through 100. Values below 20 are `"low"`; 20 through 79 are `"usable"`; 80 through 100 are `"full"`.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Mark the two cutoffs before coding.
Only the first matching branch runs.
Once the low branch is ruled out, the next branch already knows the reading is at least 20.

missions.title: Group access rules

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: When rules mix alternatives and blockers, group the alternatives before applying the shared blocker. Parentheses document the policy, even when another expression could produce the same answer.
lesson.code:
member = True
guest_pass = False
closed = True
print((member or guest_pass) and not closed)  # False

missions.brief: Return whether someone may edit a document.
requirements: Inputs are Booleans. An owner or editor may edit only when the document is not locked. A lock blocks everyone, including owners.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
missions.example:
can_edit(True, False, False) -> True
can_edit(False, True, False) -> True
hints: Which rule applies to both kinds of permitted user?
An owner must not bypass a lock.
Treat the two access roles as one group, then apply the blocker.

missions.title: Reject an invalid request

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A guard clause handles a special case and returns early. The remaining code can then assume the guard did not apply. This often makes exceptional cases easier to see.

missions.brief: Classify a requested duration as invalid, too long, or ready.
requirements: Inputs are integers and `available` is non-negative. `minutes <= 0` returns `"invalid"`. Otherwise `minutes > available` returns `"too long"`; all other requests return `"ready"`.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Which case should end the function before a normal request is considered?
Return ends the current call immediately.
After rejecting invalid duration, compare the remaining request with available time.

missions.title: Recognize a command

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `lower()` returns lowercase text. The `in` operator checks membership: for strings it checks whether one string occurs inside another. Exact command choices are better expressed as explicit equality alternatives here, since a substring is not necessarily a whole command.
lesson.code:
word = "  RADIO  "
print(word.strip().lower())  # radio
print("ad" in "radio")    # True

missions.brief: Return whether a command names a direction.
requirements: `command` is text. Ignore surrounding whitespace and letter case. Only `"north"`, `"south"`, `"east"`, and `"west"` count. Empty text and partial words are not valid. Return a Boolean.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Normalize the text once before checking its meaning.
A substring match can accept a partial word by mistake.
Use exact equality for each accepted word; an alternative collection-based check will become natural in the lists chapter.

reference.code:
def is_direction(command):
    clean = command.strip().lower()
    return clean == "north" or clean == "south" or clean == "east" or clean == "west"

print(is_direction(' NORTH '))
notes: This uses only text methods and Boolean comparisons already introduced.
After collections, membership in a collection of whole words is another clear option.

missions.title: Do the intervals meet?

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: Some decisions involve two ranges instead of one value. Draw simple intervals on paper before coding, including one that just touches another. The contract decides whether touching counts.
lesson.code:
left = 3
right = 8
point = 8
print(left <= point <= right)  # True

missions.brief: Return whether two inclusive intervals overlap.
requirements: All inputs are integers; `start_a <= end_a` and `start_b <= end_b`. Sharing one endpoint counts as overlap. Single-point intervals are valid. Return a Boolean.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: First picture the ways intervals can be completely separate.
Containment and touching both count as overlap.

missions.title: Build a dispatch decision
missions.concepts: Chapter project - priorities and Boolean policy

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A useful policy defines what happens when several conditions apply at once. Priority is part of the specification. Test combinations, not only one blocker at a time.

missions.brief: Build the status decision for a simulated session dispatcher.
requirements: `minutes` is an integer; `available` is a non-negative integer; connected and `maintenance` are Booleans.

Return one label using this priority: invalid duration (`minutes <= 0`) -`>` `"invalid"`; maintenance on -`>` `"maintenance"`; disconnected -`>` `"offline"`; duration above available -`>` `"over budget"`; otherwise -`>` `"ready"`.
An exact budget fit is ready if no higher-priority blocker applies. This is a simulation; it does not control hardware.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
missions.example:
dispatch_status(20, 20, True, False) -> 'ready'
dispatch_status(0, 0, False, True) -> 'invalid'
hints: Try an input with two simultaneous blockers.
The first applicable rule owns the answer.
A sequence of guarded returns can mirror the stated priority without deeply nested code.
